title: Angry Andy

jokes.text: Jim has been tracking Phyllis's 12 rain clichés and promised hot chocolate if she hits them all by noon
jokes.setup: It's raining and Phyllis starts saying things like 'holy moly' and 'it is raining cats and dogs'
jokes.punchline: Jim reveals he's catalogued her 12 rain clichés and has a bet riding on her completing the set
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim prank energy — low-stakes, patient, affectionate. The idea that Phyllis has exactly 12 rain clichés Jim has memorized is specific enough to feel real and is a strong character bit for both of them. The premise rewards attention and sets up a fun payoff later.

jokes.text: Jim deadpans 'You don't say?' in response to Phyllis's rain clichés while secretly tracking them
jokes.setup: Phyllis says 'Nobody knows how to drive in the rain' — a cliché Jim is covertly cataloguing
jokes.punchline: Jim's feigned interested response 'You don't say?' while secretly counting down her clichés
jokes.explanation: Short, economical, very Jim. The layers — he's pretending to be interested while secretly running a con — make the deadpan land better in context. Stronger on rewatch when you know the bit.

jokes.text: Jim desperately tries to bait Phyllis into saying the final cliché ('curled up with a good book') by asking if she wants to be 'doing something... cozy in the rain'
jokes.setup: Only one cliché left and the clock is nearly at noon — Jim tries to engineer her saying it
jokes.punchline: Jim's increasingly unsubtle prompts ('aren't some things just so nice and cozy in the rain?') as he panics
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the running bit. Jim breaking from cool detachment into active baiting is funny and in character — he can't help himself when the prank is on the line.

jokes.text: Phyllis unknowingly delivers the final cliché — 'normally the rain would make me want to stay at home, curled up with a good book' — just after noon, but says it because everyone's been so nice to her today
jokes.setup: Jim has been fishing for the cliché; Phyllis says it of her own accord, just after the deadline, framing it as a compliment to her coworkers
jokes.punchline: She completes the set naturally, unaware she's been played all morning, and the irony is that Jim's niceness is what made her happy enough to stay — defeating his own trick
jokes.explanation: Genuinely satisfying payoff. The structural irony — Jim's prank being thwarted by the warmth it accidentally generated — is elegant and very Office. The joke earns its runtime. Phyllis is the most lovable punchline here.

jokes.text: Kevin thanks Nellie for the sweater but adds 'I just wish there was pockets'
jokes.setup: Andy compliments Kevin's new sweater from Nellie as 'nice'
jokes.punchline: Kevin, grateful for the gift, delivers the backhanded critique with complete sincerity: no pockets
jokes.explanation: Compact and beautifully Kevin. He can't help but undercut a kind moment with a petty complaint, delivered with zero self-awareness. Very economical — five words do all the work. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Kevin explains that Nellie 'bobblized' his bobblehead, renaming it 'Captain Mutato'
jokes.setup: Andy asks what happened to 'Old Salty'
jokes.punchline: Nellie has renamed and apparently redesigned the bobblehead; it's now 'Captain Mutato'
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny as setup for the Kevin talking head that follows. 'Bobblize' as a verb is a small delight. Mostly setup material.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: Captain Mutato is 'half man, half mermaid. So he can fight crime as a man, and make love as a mermaid. Most of my writing involves the latter.'
jokes.setup: Kevin explains his X-Men fan fiction and the character Captain Mutato
jokes.punchline: 'Most of my writing involves the latter' — Kevin has written extensive erotic mermaid fan fiction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: the premise (half-man, half-mermaid superhero) is absurd but delivered with earnest logic. The punchline reframes all prior information — Kevin writes mostly mermaid erotica — and the delivery is perfectly restrained. It's also entirely in character: Kevin's id barely filtered through a superhero premise. 'Most of my writing involves the latter' is peak economy. Strong 8+ justification.

jokes.text: Andy introduces himself to Nellie as 'the famous Andy Bernard you've been hearing all about' in a mirror of her own greeting
jokes.setup: Nellie identifies herself as 'the famous Nellie Bertram'
jokes.punchline: Andy co-opts her phrasing to assert his own identity — slightly pathetic posturing from a man who's lost his office
jokes.explanation: A small character-comedy beat that efficiently establishes the Andy/Nellie dynamic. Andy's mirroring is both aggressive and desperate — typical of his insecure bravado.

jokes.text: Nellie's flat 'No' to Andy's politely worded request to vacate the office
jokes.setup: Andy carefully, diplomatically asks for his office back, using corporate-speak ('logistics,' 'normalcy')
jokes.punchline: Nellie's single word: 'No' — then after Andy continues, a second 'Hmm, no'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured. Andy's elaborate diplomacy is undercut by Nellie's immovable monosyllable. The repeated 'no' — especially the second 'Hmm, no' with a pondering 'hmm' — shows Nellie briefly considers it before arriving at the same answer, which is funnier than just saying no twice. Economy score near-perfect.

jokes.text: Robert talks baby care with Jim and Pam, then adds 'after Jim quiets down, you do the same thing with your baby'
jokes.setup: Robert is giving parenting advice about bicycling a baby's legs to quiet it down
jokes.punchline: Robert offhandedly compares Jim to the baby — the condescension is so casual it's almost a compliment
jokes.explanation: Very Robert California — patronizing to the point of being almost cosmic. He infantilizes Jim without any apparent malice, treating it as helpful advice. Character integration is excellent because only Robert would say this and have it land as charming rather than offensive.

jokes.text: Ryan set Kelly up with Ravi 'because Kelly is Indian, and...' then immediately backtracks: 'Race had nothing to do with it. I just knew they'd be good together. Why!'
jokes.setup: Ryan claims he set Kelly up with a pediatrician
jokes.punchline: He begins to say the quiet part loud ('because Kelly is Indian'), catches himself, and overcorrects with a defensive 'Why!' — an outraged denial of a charge nobody made
jokes.explanation: Sharp cringe comedy. Ryan's self-interruption and outrage at a question that wasn't asked is perfect characterization — he's racist and performatively progressive simultaneously. The 'Why!' is the kicker; it's defensive without being prompted.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam perform exaggerated shock at being told not to shake the baby, as if this is news to them
jokes.setup: Ravi gives the standard pediatric warning: don't shake your baby
jokes.punchline: Jim and Pam play act like this is a revelation — 'I'd never heard that before. So, thank you.' / 'Oh my God, yeah, I'm glad you said something.'
jokes.explanation: Jim and Pam's synchronized sarcasm is well-executed. The joke works because it's slightly dark (mocking a safety warning) and because their delivery stays deadpan rather than winking at the camera. Good Jim-and-Pam team comedy.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'Kelly and I broke up and she can do whatever she wants. And her new boyfriend seems awesome... if you're into Indian people. I'm not.'
jokes.setup: Ryan tries to play it cool about Kelly's new boyfriend
jokes.punchline: He reveals casual racism toward Indian people — while having dated Kelly Kapoor, who is Indian, for years
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The joke's power comes from the callback to Ryan's earlier slip and the staggering hypocrisy — he dated an Indian woman for years and now claims he's 'not into Indian people.' The blunt final sentence 'I'm not' delivered deadpan is brutally funny and perfectly Ryan. Strong 8+ candidate: the character integration is exceptional, the economy is near-perfect, and it deepens the running Ryan characterization.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I'd rather she be alone than with somebody. Is that love?'
jokes.setup: Ryan reflects on seeing Kelly happy with Ravi
jokes.punchline: He describes jealousy and possessiveness and sincerely asks if that's love — unaware he's describing the opposite of love
jokes.explanation: Darkly funny character study. Ryan's complete lack of self-awareness about what love actually is, paired with his earnest question to the camera, is tragicomic. The pause before 'Is that love?' sells it.

jokes.text: Robert California, asked to mediate the Andy/Nellie office standoff, tells Nellie to 'get accustomed to' people saying no because 'then it feels good when they finally say yes'
jokes.setup: Robert is supposedly there to resolve the dispute and return the office to Andy
jokes.punchline: Instead of helping Andy, Robert gives Nellie philosophy about the erotic pleasure of delayed consent — completely undermining his stated purpose
jokes.explanation: Pure Robert California: he cannot give a straight business response without filtering it through erotic philosophy. His immediate abandonment of Andy's cause in favor of life wisdom is both funny and revealing. Strong character integration — only Robert says this.

jokes.text: Robert's talking head about sexual desire influencing business decisions: 'I never allow sexual desire to influence a business decision. So I find it best to recuse myself temporarily until I've had a chance to make love, and then go back and analyze the situation rationally. Buffett operates the same way.'
jokes.setup: Robert explains his recusal from the Andy/Nellie dispute
jokes.punchline: His 'rational' method is to have sex first, then decide — and he attributes this to Warren Buffett
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a summit of Robert California characterization. The joke works on multiple levels: the pseudo-rational framing of profoundly irrational behavior, the corporate-speak ('recuse myself temporarily'), and the closing Buffett name-drop delivered with complete sincerity. Only Robert California could say 'I recuse myself until I've made love' with the gravity of business advice. Strong 8.5 justification: exceptional character integration, great structure, highly quotable, economical.

jokes.text: Andy counts down from five to dock Nellie's pay, Nellie calls his bluff ('You can't dock my pay'), Andy escalates to calling for Angela — then finds Angela won't dock Nellie's pay either
jokes.setup: Andy threatens to dock Nellie's pay $100 if she doesn't vacate the office in a five-second countdown
jokes.punchline: Nellie points out he lacks the authority; Andy tries to use Angela as enforcer; Angela ignores him for Nellie
jokes.explanation: The escalating futility is funny — Andy weaponizes the only tool he has (Angela's compliance) and finds it no longer works. Good setup for the extended sequence that follows.

jokes.text: The countdown escalation: Andy and Nellie go through multiple five-count cycles, with Andy docking increasingly absurd amounts, culminating in '$10,000,' while Nellie taunts 'you're just saying numbers'
jokes.setup: Andy's repeated countdowns have been producing nothing but larger dollar amounts docked from Nellie
jokes.punchline: Nellie reduces the whole thing: 'It's literally like... you're just saying numbers.' Andy threatens $10,000.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation comedy. Nellie's meta-commentary ('you're just saying numbers') is the best line of the sequence — she articulates exactly why the bit is funny, which doubles back and makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Andy and Erin's mutual reassurance that last night 'was not a big deal' and both were 'just tired' — played as obviously a big deal
jokes.setup: Andy and Erin talk about the previous night with forced casualness
jokes.punchline: Both overcorrect — Erin says Andy was 'so sexy' with suspicious enthusiasm; Andy's 'Yeah. I know it's not... a big deal' talking head clearly indicates it IS a very big deal
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup for what becomes the episode's main B-plot. Both actors play the subtext well. Not a laugh-out-loud moment but effective comedic foundation.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: clearly devastated, saying 'Yeah. I know it's not... a big deal' about his sexual performance issue with a pained pause
jokes.setup: Andy has been reassured it's not a big deal
jokes.punchline: His talking head confirms it is absolutely a big deal to him — the pause before 'a big deal' does all the work
jokes.explanation: The pause is the joke. Andy's devastation leaking through his forced casualness is well-performed. The talking-head format makes his self-deception visible and comedic.

jokes.text: Pam says the photo was taken 'right before we got in that huge fight'; Ryan says he doesn't remember the fight, only how pretty Pam looked taking pictures of him
jokes.setup: Looking at old photos from a weekend trip together
jokes.punchline: Ryan's romantic-sounding recollection is entirely self-centered — he was looking at himself being photographed, not at Pam
jokes.explanation: Sharp Ryan moment. The apparent romance — 'how pretty you looked' — is subverted by 'taking those pictures of me.' He's narcisstically complimenting himself for being photographed. Classic Ryan selfishness with economy.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I'm in love with Kelly Kapoor... all I can think about is spending the rest of my life with her. Again, that could change.'
jokes.setup: Ryan delivers a heartfelt profession of love for Kelly
jokes.punchline: 'Again, that could change.' — he undercuts his entire declaration with casual hedging
jokes.explanation: One of the tightest jokes in the episode. The construction is textbook: build a genuine emotional statement, then demolish it with the minimum possible words. 'Again, that could change' is brilliant because 'again' implies this has been established before, and 'could change' is so casual it doubles the comedy. Pure Ryan. Strong 8+ justification: perfect economy, excellent structure, maximum character integration.

jokes.text: Erin's talking head about Andy losing the manager job: 'I don't know what the technical term is. Hmm. Penial... softiosis.'
jokes.setup: Erin is asked if losing the manager job affected Andy 'outside the office'
jokes.punchline: Erin invents a medical-sounding term for erectile dysfunction — 'penial softiosis' — delivered with genuine uncertainty about whether she's got the right word
jokes.explanation: Excellent Erin joke. 'Penial softiosis' is a perfect malapropism — it sounds almost medical, Erin delivers it with a thoughtful 'hmm' as if reaching for the right term, and it's funny because she's neither embarrassed nor entirely wrong. The made-up word is the joke, and 'softiosis' has a sad poetry to it. Strong character integration: only Erin would coin this term with this much sincerity.

jokes.text: Robert California denies ever experiencing anything 'remotely like that,' then immediately starts listing erection-adjacent monuments: 'Washington Monument.' 'Okay.' 'Eiffel Tower.' 'Okay, okay.'
jokes.setup: Robert is assuring Erin he's never had performance issues.
jokes.punchline: He punctuates his denial by citing the Washington Monument and Eiffel Tower — apparently the visual metaphors he uses to describe his erections, delivered as if this is perfectly normal.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Robert California absurdist comedy. The sudden pivot to phallic landmark names is completely unexpected and delivered with his characteristic grandiosity — as if naming great monuments of the world is simply how one discusses one's virility. The 'Okay, okay' response from Erin trying to keep up is perfectly timed. Very quotable and highly original within the episode context.

jokes.text: Kelly responds to Ryan pointing out he cheated on her with 'Which time?'
jokes.setup: Pam tells Kelly to remember how it felt when Ryan cheated on her
jokes.punchline: Kelly's 'Which time?' — casual, not even angry, just clarifying
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect. 'Which time?' does everything: it confirms Ryan is a serial cheater, shows Kelly has normalized it, makes Pam's intervention look naive, and gets the laugh entirely through economy. Near-perfect structure for a two-word joke. Genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I'm not going to let Kelly throw her life away on Ryan... I mean Ravi.' Then adds he's not trying to get access to the pediatrician.
jokes.setup: Ryan explains why he's intervening in Kelly's relationship
jokes.punchline: He accidentally says his own name instead of Ravi's — revealing his solipsism — and then preemptively denies the pediatrician motive
jokes.explanation: The self-name slip is a great character moment — Ryan literally centers himself in every thought. The follow-up denial of the pediatrician angle is good too because we hadn't yet thought to ask. Compact and character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight's briefing for Nellie: 'One of Toby's eyes is getting smaller. So there's that.' — delivered with deadpan gravitas as an intelligence report
jokes.setup: Dwight is giving Nellie his daily intelligence briefing on office happenings
jokes.punchline: The briefing includes Toby's apparently shrinking eye as an item of interest — 'so there's that' is the perfect non-committal conclusion
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Dwight moment. His role as Nellie's informer is funny in itself; the actual intelligence is Toby's asymmetric eye situation delivered with journalistic neutrality. 'So there's that' is perfectly understated. Dwight's self-importance as spy/briefer combined with the triviality of the intel makes this land. Strong 8 justification.

jokes.text: Dwight's briefing continues: Gabe bragged about an air show ticket to Meredith, then immediately said his friend might take it — 'so I'll keep you posted on that'
jokes.setup: Dwight is briefing Nellie on Gabe's social failures
jokes.punchline: Gabe advertised a social opportunity, got a nibble, then immediately pulled the invitation back — Dwight treats this as actionable intel and promises follow-up reporting
jokes.explanation: Gabe's sad social maneuver (invite then retract) is funny, and Dwight's treating it as serious intelligence worth following is funnier. Slightly weaker than the Toby's eye item but still good.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals to Nellie that Andy couldn't perform sexually: 'Oh, and Andy lost his masculinity, so congratulations on that.' / 'By contrast, I went to sleep with an erection so large it was like I was wearing no blanket at all.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's intelligence briefing for Nellie — includes a report on Andy's sexual dysfunction
jokes.punchline: Dwight contrasts Andy's failure with his own impressive erection, described with farming-level matter-of-factness: 'like I was wearing no blanket at all'
jokes.explanation: The episode's standout joke alongside Robert's Buffett line. 'Like I was wearing no blanket at all' is extraordinary — it's specific, visual, practical (of course Dwight would measure in terms of blanket coverage), and so anatomically matter-of-fact that it's both horrifying and hilarious. The delivery as a coda to an intelligence briefing, prefaced by 'congratulations on that' to Nellie, makes it even better. Exceptional character integration: only Dwight Schrute delivers this line in this way. Strong 8.5+ justification.

jokes.text: Nellie responds to Dwight's erection report: 'Wow, I knew you'd win, but you just demolished him! I'm a little bit jealous, actually. Reduced him to a mere ant.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has reported his superior erection to Nellie in clinical terms
jokes.punchline: Nellie reacts as though this were a sporting competition — 'you just demolished him' — and expresses jealousy that she didn't win the contest
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat. Nellie framing the erection report as a competitive demolition adds another comic layer. 'Reduced him to a mere ant' is a funny over-reach. Mostly riffs on Dwight's setup.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I just wanted to take the man's job, not his manhood.'
jokes.setup: Nellie celebrates Dwight's 'victory' over Andy
jokes.punchline: Dwight expresses unexpected and almost honorable regret — he never meant to destroy Andy this completely
jokes.explanation: Sharp and economical. The parallel structure ('the job, not his manhood') is clean. There's also a hint of Dwight's strange honorability — he has a code, and destroying someone's manhood wasn't on the agenda. Quotable.

jokes.text: Andy attempts to call a meeting, Nellie says 'you can't call a meeting,' Andy repeats himself louder — then thanks everyone for coming to 'my meeting'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to exercise managerial authority by calling a meeting
jokes.punchline: Nellie denies his authority; Andy simply repeats louder and asserts ownership of the meeting anyway
jokes.explanation: Decent character comedy about Andy's desperate assertion of authority. The 'thank you for coming to my meeting' is the best beat — he's claimed the territory verbally even if not actually.

jokes.text: Nellie corrects Andy mid-meeting: 'Andrew, not everyone here is important. And the word is impotence. Which is important in its own way.'
jokes.setup: Andy is saying each person is 'vitally important'
jokes.punchline: Nellie points out his verbal slip — 'important' sounds like 'impotent' — and outs his meeting's real topic while correcting his grammar
jokes.explanation: Excellent wordplay moment. The important/impotence near-homophone is a genuine find, and 'which is important in its own way' doubles back beautifully. Nellie weaponizes grammar correction as humiliation. The structure is tight and the punchline lands on the twist of the word. Strong beat.

jokes.text: Andy's 'meeting' response: 'Take a man's job, but leave him his balls.' Margaret Thatcher said that... probably. Don't know. Don't read. Didn't see the movie.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to respond to Nellie's impotence accusation with dignity
jokes.punchline: He invokes Thatcher as an authority on masculine pride, immediately undermines it with 'probably,' then admits he's illiterate and hasn't seen the biopic
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy joke. The structure escalates brilliantly: confident Thatcher attribution → 'probably' → admitting he doesn't read → admitting he didn't see the movie. The self-defeating cascade is perfectly Andy — he starts with false authority and dismantles it himself in real-time. 'Don't read' delivered flatly is the best beat. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Nellie informs the group: 'Flounders frequently experience impotence, especially when converting from male to female and then back again to male.'
jokes.setup: Andy says impotence is 'a human problem'; Nellie wants to expand the discussion
jokes.punchline: Nellie corrects Andy's human-centric view by citing flounder sex-change biology with scientific confidence
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully absurd. The specificity of 'when converting from male to female and then back again to male' sells it — it sounds just plausible enough. Nellie's earnest commitment to expanding the impotence conversation into ichthyology is very on-brand for her character's odd confidence. The joke requires biological facts that are amusingly specific.

jokes.text: Nellie clarifies the impotence meeting is 'not me': 'I've never had any problem in that arena. And I have been with several older men.'
jokes.setup: People assume the meeting is about Nellie's sexual problem
jokes.punchline: Nellie's overshare — she categorically denies personal dysfunction and offers her history with older men as evidence, with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Good overshare joke. 'I have been with several older men' as a defense feels very Nellie — she provides evidence from her personal history without any embarrassment, which is funnier than if she'd been coy about it.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight simultaneously ask 'How old?' and then Jim calls jinx
jokes.setup: Nellie reveals she's been with several older men
jokes.punchline: Jim and Dwight's synchronized prurient curiosity, then Jim's 'Jinx. Buy me some coke.'
jokes.explanation: The 'jinx' bit is a quick laugh. Jim and Dwight's unexpected alignment on wanting to know is a nice side-effect. Economy is good; the bit doesn't overstay.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals it was Andy who had the impotence problem after promising to keep it secret
jokes.setup: People are speculating who in the room has the impotence problem; Dwight was sworn to secrecy
jokes.punchline: Dwight breaks and says 'Dwight told me about it earlier' — then backtracks when confronted, only to accidentally confirm it
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. The Dwight-outing-himself-while-trying-to-deflect is well-executed though not surprising given his character.

jokes.text: Andy finally admits his impotence publicly: 'Fine, it was me. I couldn't-- I had a problem with Erin last night. Happy?'
jokes.setup: The meeting has devolved into chaos; Andy is now the obvious subject
jokes.punchline: Andy breaks, self-outs, and turns it into an aggrieved question to the room
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'Happy?' directed at the assembled crowd is a good note. The reluctant confession followed by defiant indignation is well-played, character-consistent.

jokes.text: Andy's complaint: 'It's usually not followed by a giant workplace discussion and an interview.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just publicly admitted his impotence
jokes.punchline: He notes with exasperation that impotence normally doesn't lead to a full conference room discussion AND a documentary camera interview — a wink at the mockumentary format
jokes.explanation: Nice meta moment. Andy's acknowledgment of the talking-head interview as part of his humiliation is a good self-aware gag for the format. The Office rarely does meta this explicitly, so it stands out.

jokes.text: Dwight polls the room for impotence solidarity: 'Tuna. T-dog!' / Jim: 'I have other issues. I'm terrible at math. Overweight.' / Dwight: 'You're in great shape.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants every man to admit they've had impotence to make Andy feel better
jokes.punchline: Jim deflects with completely unrelated complaints about himself; Dwight sincerely corrects the 'overweight' claim, missing the joke entirely
jokes.explanation: Good Jim/Dwight dynamic. Jim's evasion by listing unrelated flaws is clever, and Dwight's earnest correction of 'overweight' — 'You're in great shape, a lot better shape than I am' — is funny because he's trying to be encouraging while completely missing that Jim is dodging the question.

jokes.text: Kevin defends Erin's sex life: 'Erin doesn't even like sex, remember? You said it feels like getting tackled by a skeleton.'
jokes.setup: People are discussing Andy's problem; Kevin tries to minimize it
jokes.punchline: Kevin reveals Erin's private description of sex — 'getting tackled by a skeleton' — with zero awareness of how inappropriate this is
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best line. 'Getting tackled by a skeleton' is an extraordinary piece of writing: it's specific, grotesque, physical, and perfectly Erin (skinny, vulnerable, slightly otherworldly). Kevin delivering it as a helpful intervention — trying to remove the pressure on Andy — while destroying both Erin's privacy and dignity is peak Kevin. The image is so vivid and strange it becomes instantly quotable. Exceptional originality and economy. This is a line that people remember.

jokes.text: Dwight asks 'Chumbo, come on, help me out. Any problems with little Chumbo?' — apparently having a pet name for his own genitalia
jokes.setup: Dwight is polling the room for impotence confessions to support Andy
jokes.punchline: Dwight has apparently named a part of himself 'Chumbo' and refers to it in the third person with casual familiarity
jokes.explanation: Very Dwight. The casual naming of anatomy, the third-person address, and the polling framing all work together. 'Tip-top shape' as the reply (from someone, possibly himself) rounds it out. The self-assurance is perfect Dwight character comedy.

jokes.text: Creed: 'Haven't heard any complaints. Wouldn't care if I did.'
jokes.setup: Dwight asks Creed — who Andy has pointed out is '1,000 years old' — if he has any impotence issues
jokes.punchline: Creed's two-sentence response: supremely confident about his sexual performance, and utterly indifferent to partner feedback
jokes.explanation: Perfect Creed joke. Two sentences, maximum information density. The first clause ('Haven't heard any complaints') sets up normal confidence; the second ('Wouldn't care if I did') transforms it into something much darker and funnier. It's the sociopathic edge that makes Creed lines special. Character integration is near-perfect — this is quintessentially Creed. Strong 8.5 justification.

jokes.text: Jim's reluctant impotence confession: 'Yes, that time that it was very late... We'd had sex so many times already, I was exhausted. I could barely see. I was very drunk.'
jokes.setup: Jim is pressured by the whole room to share an impotence experience to help Andy
jokes.punchline: Jim's story reveals so many mitigating circumstances piled on each other (late, exhausted, already had sex many times, couldn't see, drunk) that it stops being sympathetic to Andy and becomes a brag
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. The cumulative excuses become funnier as they pile up — each one supposedly making the moment more relatable but actually making Jim sound like he's bragging. Pam's 'Okay, stop' is the best beat.

jokes.text: Meredith's confession: 'If it makes you feel any better, I never had an orgasm until I was 42. And then when I did, it lasted till I was 44. 43 was ju-- I got nothing done.'
jokes.setup: People are sharing intimate struggles to make Andy feel better
jokes.punchline: Meredith had a two-year orgasm. '43 was ju-- I got nothing done.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic peak. Meredith's two-year orgasm is a perfectly escalating absurdity — the setup (didn't have one until 42) is sympathetic, then the punchline reveals she's been in one continuously for two years, and the kicker '43 was ju-- I got nothing done' is the perfect beat. The interruption ('ju--') implies she started to describe the height of it and gave up — and the practical complaint ('I got nothing done') is genius economy. This is the kind of joke that defines a character. Highest craft score in the episode.

jokes.text: Dwight suggests prostate stimulation as a solution, then claims he heard it on 'This American Life'
jokes.setup: Dwight offers to help with a medical solution to impotence
jokes.punchline: He recommends rectal stimulation, then distances himself from personal knowledge by attributing it to a public radio show
jokes.explanation: The 'This American Life' attribution is the joke — Dwight claiming a respectable NPR source for something clearly personal. The 'I don't know anything about this personally' tells us exactly the opposite.

jokes.text: Dwight offers to rent Andy his 'rectal electro-ejaculator' — which is 'rated for bovine use only'
jokes.setup: The prostate stimulation discussion continues; Dwight has a practical solution
jokes.punchline: Dwight owns a rectal electro-ejaculator that he uses on cattle and would rent to Andy at a presumably competitive price
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight joke. 'Rated for bovine use only' is the perfect modifier — it tells us Dwight has this device for legitimate farm use (of course he does) and is offering a service extension, not lending a personal item. The rental framing ('I could let you rent it') adds a practical Dwight touch. The specificity of 'electro-ejaculator' is the kind of medical-technical term that rewards the absurdity. Strong 8+ justification: only Dwight owns and offers this device with this casual generosity.

jokes.text: Andy asks if Toby can stop the meeting: 'Toby, doesn't HR have some rules against talking about this kind of stuff?' Erin responds: 'HR is a joke. I can't do anything about anything.'
jokes.setup: Andy appeals to HR authority to shut down the humiliating meeting
jokes.punchline: Toby (via Erin's words) confirms HR is powerless — delivered with apparent dejected acceptance
jokes.explanation: Good Toby joke. The long-running Toby-as-powerless-HR-drone is well-served here. 'HR is a joke' from the HR rep himself is the key beat — Toby's self-awareness about his own irrelevance is always funny.

jokes.text: Andy, on phone with his dad, says: 'Dad, don't think of it as a demotion. Just think of it as a promotion to a lower level.'
jokes.setup: Andy is calling his father, apparently to explain being demoted back to sales
jokes.punchline: 'A promotion to a lower level' — Andy's spin is internally contradictory and shows his desperate need to save face with his father
jokes.explanation: Sharp character moment. 'A promotion to a lower level' is a beautifully constructed oxymoron that reveals Andy's self-deception and his fraught relationship with his father. The logic fails immediately but he says it with conviction. Quotable and economical.

jokes.text: Nellie corrects Erin's date format on phone memos: 'I prefer it day, month, year. Small, bigger, biggest.' Then adds: 'Oh, sexual innuendo. Not intentional. Shut up!'
jokes.setup: Nellie gives Erin a mundane administrative correction about date formatting
jokes.punchline: Nellie catches her own double entendre ('small, bigger, biggest' in the context of the day's impotence discussion) and yells at no one in particular to shut up
jokes.explanation: Good moment. Nellie catching herself mid-double-entendre and yelling 'Shut up!' at the implied laughter is well-constructed. The self-aware shame is funny because she's the one who brought it up. 'Not intentional' delivered quickly makes it more believable and therefore funnier.

jokes.text: Erin's angry outburst: tells Nellie to take the memos herself, outs Andy's sexual performance issue to the whole office ('our sex life is none of your business!'), and declares 'Andy is the manager, not Nellie!'
jokes.setup: Nellie has been making small corrections to Erin's work; Erin snaps
jokes.punchline: Erin's defense of Andy ironically reveals everything she was trying to protect by publicly shouting about 'our sex life'
jokes.explanation: Good cringe moment. Erin's passionate defense destroys the privacy she was defending. The classic sitcom irony of saying the quiet part loud while trying to protect it.

jokes.text: Andy's meltdown: 'Stop protecting me. I'm a man -- I can protect myself.' Then to his phone: 'Dad, go to hell! I'm taller than you!'
jokes.setup: Andy is humiliated by Erin's public defense and is trying to assert manhood
jokes.punchline: 'Dad, go to hell! I'm taller than you!' — Andy's father-directed rage arrives mid-meltdown, with the height detail revealing childhood wounds
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'Dad, go to hell! I'm taller than you!' is a perfect comedic non-sequitur — Andy's rage at his father suddenly finding the specific grievance of height reveals an entire childhood dynamic in six words. The escalation from professional humiliation to Oedipal height battle is both absurd and deeply sad. Strong 8+ justification: highly quotable, great economy, specific to Andy's character, and the 'I'm taller than you' detail is genuinely inspired writing.

jokes.text: After Andy runs into the wall, a colleague deadpans: 'He does not like that wall.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just physically attacked a wall in rage
jokes.punchline: The understatement — as if Andy has a pre-existing beef with the wall — is the joke
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan understatement after a big physical beat. The line works because it deflates the drama instantly and implies a personal history between Andy and walls. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: After Andy's rage meltdown, Dwight casually says: 'Maybe we'll get sent to anger management together. That would actually be cool. I'd love for you to meet some of the guys.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just gone berserk in the office
jokes.punchline: Dwight treats Andy's breakdown as an opportunity for social bonding — he has an established anger management social group with regulars ('the guys')
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The information that Dwight has an established social circle at anger management — 'the guys' — is extraordinary. He's excited at the prospect of Andy joining this group, treating a breakdown as a networking opportunity. The 'that would actually be cool' is the pivot from sympathy to enthusiasm that makes it. Strong 8.5 justification: excellent character integration (Dwight's anger management group is a perfect Dwight detail), great structure, highly quotable, and the line reframes Dwight's character beautifully.

jokes.text: Ryan confronts Pam: 'If you have something bad to say to me, say it to my face.' Pam: 'Fair enough. Um... I don't think you're a very good person. And forgive me, but I feel like I've said this to you before.'
jokes.setup: Ryan challenges Pam to say bad things to his face
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately obliges with calm, devastating directness — and notes she's had to say this before
jokes.explanation: Sharp Pam moment. 'I don't think you're a very good person' is delivered with the calm of stating a fact — no heat, just clarity — and the 'I feel like I've said this to you before' makes it worse for Ryan. Pam's deadpan as a weapon is underused in the show and lands here. Good structure: Ryan sets up the invitation, Pam takes it exactly as offered.

jokes.text: Brian from the documentary crew chimes in about Ravi: 'just having knowing you short while, Brian, that I prefer Ravi. And again, I've never even met the guy.'
jokes.setup: Multiple people prefer Ravi to Ryan for Kelly, including someone who has never met Ravi
jokes.punchline: Even a near-stranger — the documentary crew member Brian — prefers an unknown man to Ryan based solely on knowing Ryan
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation of Ryan's universal rejection. The logic — 'knowing you is enough to prefer a stranger' — is the joke, and it's well-executed. The 'And again, I've never even met the guy' is a good kicker.

jokes.text: Ryan claims to have written an 'amazing love poem' for Kelly but says he can't read it because 'my heart couldn't handle it.' When pressed: 'This poem would crush you!'
jokes.setup: Ryan is trying to win Kelly back with a poem
jokes.punchline: The poem is so amazing it would be physically dangerous to read — a self-aggrandizing refusal that implies the poem doesn't exist or is terrible
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ryan gambit. The escalating refusal ('my heart couldn't handle it' → 'read through the pain' → 'This poem would crush you!') is a wonderful exercise in Ryan's narcissism. He's made his nonexistent poem so mythologized that reading it becomes heroic suffering. Very in character.

jokes.text: Ryan claims to have written Kelly 'the most amazing love poem' but says he can't read it because 'my heart couldn't handle it.' When pressed, he says 'This poem would crush you!'
jokes.setup: Ryan is trying to win Kelly back with a love poem.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's poem is so good he can't even read it himself — a grandiose, self-aggrandizing pose that serves as his primary seduction tactic.
jokes.explanation: Good Ryan posturing joke. 'This poem would crush you!' is the right hyperbolic escalation. His refusal to read it (because it's too emotionally powerful for him) is a perfect transparent manipulation that works as character comedy.

jokes.text: Kelly's talking head: 'Ravi makes me incredibly happy. And Ryan puts me through so much drama. So I guess I just have to decide which of those is more important to me.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is deciding between Ravi and Ryan
jokes.punchline: She frames the obvious choice (happiness vs. drama) as a genuine dilemma — the joke being that Kelly has always chosen drama and isn't sure she shouldn't again
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Kelly. The fact that she has to genuinely think about whether 'happiness' or 'drama' is more important reveals everything about her character. The deadpan delivery of an obviously absurd consideration is the joke.

jokes.text: Robert California tells Andy: 'I promise you, in time, we'll all laugh about this incident.' Andy: 'I already think it's kinda funny.'
jokes.setup: Robert is trying to soften the blow of Andy's demotion.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate 'I already think it's kinda funny' — said with genuine lightness — subverts the expected emotional reaction.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective beat. Andy's genuine lightness about the situation — which contradicts his entire arc in the episode — is a nice character surprise. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Robert California is told Andy said 'No' to demotion; Robert tells Andy if he says no one more time he's fired. Andy's response: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Robert California warns Andy that one more 'no' means termination
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately says 'No' — not from stupidity but from a new, almost Zen resolve
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural callback. Nellie's 'No' has been the episode's running bit from her side; now Andy deploys it at maximum consequence. Robert sets up the ultimatum with perfect clarity, which makes Andy's monosyllabic defiance land harder. The economy (one word) combined with the stakes makes this one of the episode's strongest beats. Justified 8+.

jokes.text: Robert California, having just fired Andy, walks away — and Pam's reaction is 'Boo! Boo to you!'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been fired for refusing the demotion
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'Boo! Boo!' reaction — childlike, sincere, and totally disproportionate for a workplace firing
jokes.explanation: Charming but not a particularly crafted joke. Pam's booing is funny for its kindergarten energy in a corporate moment, but it's more character warmth than comedy craft.

jokes.text: Ryan's marriage proposal: 'I wanna marry you, Kelly Kapoor. Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow. But someday. And probably.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is making a heartfelt proposal to win Kelly back
jokes.punchline: 'And probably' — he hedges the 'someday' with a probability qualifier, destroying the romance while apparently not noticing
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ryan joke, companion to his 'again, that could change' line. 'And probably' is two syllables that demolish the preceding romantic structure. It's not even a hedge — it's a probability estimate. The escalating de-commitment (today → tomorrow → someday → probably) is perfectly structured. Ryan's inability to commit to his own proposal is peak Ryan and very quotable. Strong 8+ justification.

jokes.text: Pam yells 'Barf! Ugh, you suck!' at Ryan's proposal — then the old woman in the convertible refuses to turn her car around for Ryan
jokes.setup: Ryan is making his grand romantic speech to Kelly, appealing to passersby for a cinematic backdrop
jokes.punchline: The old woman ('Betsy') won't turn her convertible around for Ryan's proposal; multiple people have to beg her; she still won't
jokes.explanation: Decent physical comedy bit. 'She don't wanna turn around' is a good beat — even strangers are rejecting Ryan. Funny but broad.

jokes.text: Ryan physically tries to turn a bus or vehicle around to face Kelly, demanding help: 'Can we turn this back around quickly, please? Help me turn this fucking thing around, please. Thank you. She don't wanna turn around.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is trying to have a dramatic romantic moment while something (a vehicle/bus) isn't cooperating.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's grand romantic gesture is physically foiled by an inanimate object, and his desperate cursing at it while trying to maintain romantic momentum is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that plays better visually than it reads in transcript. Ryan trying to maintain romantic dignity while fighting with an uncooperative vehicle is solid broad comedy. 'She don't wanna turn around' personifying the vehicle is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Ryan's proposal clause: 'I can't promise you that I'll never cheat on you. Nor should I. Modern marriages aren't built that way. Men aren't built that way. There's a very interesting article I can email to you.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is delivering what he believes to be a sincere and romantic marriage proposal
jokes.punchline: He explicitly disclaims fidelity as a promise, provides sociological justification, and offers to send supporting reading materials
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes, on par with the Buffett line and the blanket erection. Ryan's proposal includes a formal disclaimer of fidelity followed by pseudo-intellectual justification ('Modern marriages aren't built that way. Men aren't built that way.') and a reference to an article he can email. The escalation from bad to worse is perfect, and 'There's a very interesting article I can email to you' is a masterpiece of character economy — it's so Ryan that it barely needs a laugh track. Strong 8.5 justification.

jokes.text: Ryan's closing proposal line: 'Even if the odds are 50/50 that we'll break up within the week, I wanna roll those dice. I love you, Kelly. Ryan. Will you roll those dice with me?'
jokes.setup: Ryan is concluding his romantic proposal to Kelly
jokes.punchline: He frames their love as a 50/50 coin flip on a one-week timeline and asks Kelly to 'roll those dice' — the most unromantic romantic appeal possible
jokes.explanation: Ryan's proposal ends with specific, pessimistic actuarial thinking — 50/50 odds of breaking up within a week — as his rallying cry. 'Will you roll those dice with me?' is the best kind of terrible romance. The callback to 'roll those dice' after establishing the terrible odds makes it funnier. Character integration near-perfect: only Ryan proposes with statistics this specific and this bad.

jokes.text: After Kelly rejects Ryan and asks for a hug, Ryan stares blankly and says 'What?' then 'This was really cool.'
jokes.setup: Kelly has chosen Ravi over Ryan and offered a consolation hug
jokes.punchline: Ryan's 'What?' suggests he can't process rejection, then 'This was really cool' — his immediate reframe into casual detachment
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Ryan's 'This was really cool' — pivoting from rejected suitor to detached participant — is perfectly him. The 'What?' pause before it is important: he needed a second to find his persona. Economy is high; four words do the character work.

jokes.text: Ryan's 'What?' reaction to Kelly's hug request — visual beat
jokes.setup: Kelly has just asked Ryan for a hug after rejecting his proposal
jokes.punchline: Ryan's single 'What?' captures his complete inability to process the social request in context
jokes.explanation: One word, total punctuation. 'What?' from Ryan in this context says everything about how thoroughly Kelly has wrong-footed him. Works as a beat-completion to #64.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'Well, it's good to see Kelly's maturing.'
jokes.setup: Kelly has just chosen the stable, loving Ravi over Ryan — the sensible choice
jokes.punchline: Pam frames it as a maturity milestone — implying that choosing the obviously better partner is Kelly's first adult decision
jokes.explanation: Short, clean, slightly condescending Pam observation. The low bar for 'maturing' is the implicit joke. Efficient but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head after being fired: 'I can't describe it. I just, for the first time in a long time, I actually feel in control. I feel... alive.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been fired for refusing to be demoted
jokes.punchline: The most defeated moment of Andy's professional life makes him feel 'in control' and 'alive' — the irony is total
jokes.explanation: Good ironic character moment. Andy's self-deception reaching new heights as he finds dignity in getting fired is both funny and slightly poignant. The Office does this tragicomic blend well.

jokes.text: Andy has hurt his hand punching the wall but insists on carrying his own box: 'I got it. But you hurt your hand. I... got it.' Then he struggles visibly.
jokes.setup: Andy has been fired and is packing his desk; he has injured his hand but refuses help
jokes.punchline: Andy's stubborn masculine insistence on carrying his own stuff despite obvious injury — 'I... got it' with pained determination
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat. Andy's wounded pride manifesting as physical stubbornness is consistent with his arc. Not a standout joke but well-observed.

jokes.text: After everything, Ryan reads from his 'poem' — it's barely coherent ('Kapoor and Kadesperate. He watches... He is a drifter out to see...') — and Kelly is clearly moved despite herself
jokes.setup: Pam has convinced Ryan to read the poem; she expects it to be terrible
jokes.punchline: The poem IS terrible — incoherent and overwrought — but Kelly is moved, and Pam's final talking-head admits it got to her too: 'Ryan can never know.'
jokes.explanation: Good closing joke with emotional complexity. The poem is objectively bad ('Kadesperate') but somehow effective, and Pam's 'Ryan can never know' is a perfect coda — she's been Ryan's opponent all episode and secretly has to admit the poem moved her. The layered irony (bad poem, genuine emotion, Pam's shame) is sophisticated for a sitcom ending. The callback to Ryan's earlier refusal to read it pays off.

tmdb_overview: Andy returns to the office to find Nellie in the manager's chair. Meanwhile, Kelly struggles to choose between Ryan and a new man.
